questions.q: Let $\mathbf{u}=\langle2,-1,3\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,4,-2\rangle$. Find $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ and $3\mathbf{u}-2\mathbf{v}$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\langle3,3,1\rangle$. $3\mathbf{u}=\langle6,-3,9\rangle$, $2\mathbf{v}=\langle2,8,-4\rangle$, so $3\mathbf{u}-2\mathbf{v}=\langle4,-11,13\rangle$.

questions.q: Let $\mathbf{a}=\langle1,0,-2,3\rangle$, $\mathbf{b}=\langle-1,2,1,0\rangle$ (vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$). Find $\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}$.
questions.answer: $2\mathbf{b}=\langle-2,4,2,0\rangle$, so $\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}=\langle-1,4,3,3\rangle$.

questions.q: Solve for $\mathbf{x}$: $\mathbf{x}+\langle2,-3\rangle=\langle5,1\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{x}=\langle5,1\rangle-\langle2,-3\rangle=\langle3,4\rangle$.

questions.q: For $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,2,2\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle3,-1,0\rangle$, find $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}$ and $|\mathbf{u}|$.
Find the angle between $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,0,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,1,0\rangle$ using $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|}$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=1$, $|\mathbf{u}|=1$, $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{2}$. $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $\theta=45^\circ$ ($\pi/4$).

questions.q: For $\mathbf{u}=\langle2,2,-1\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle0,3,4\rangle$, find $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}$, $|\mathbf{u}|$, and $|\mathbf{v}|$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0+6-4=2$. $|\mathbf{u}|=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3$. $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{0+9+16}=5$.

questions.q: State the Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality.
questions.answer: For all vectors $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$: $|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|$.

questions.q: Verify the Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality for $\mathbf{u}=\langle3,4\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,2\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=3+8=11$. $|\mathbf{u}|=5$, $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{5}$, so $|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|=5\sqrt{5}\approx11.18$. Since $11 \leq 11.18$, the inequality holds (it is strict here because $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are not parallel).

questions.q: For which pairs $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$ does Cauchy–Schwarz hold with EQUALITY? Verify equality for $\mathbf{u}=\langle2,4\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,2\rangle$.
questions.answer: Equality holds exactly when $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are parallel (one is a scalar multiple of the other). Here $\mathbf{u}=2\mathbf{v}$: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=2+8=10$; $|\mathbf{u}|=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}$, $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{5}$, so $|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|=2(5)=10$. Indeed $10=10$.

questions.q: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{v}=\langle3,-4\rangle$.
questions.answer: $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. Unit vector: $\left\langle\frac{3}{5},-\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle$.

questions.q: Find a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,2,2\rangle$.
questions.answer: $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3$. Unit vector: $\left\langle\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}\right\rangle$.

questions.q: Find a vector of length $10$ in the same direction as $\mathbf{v}=\langle3,4\rangle$.
questions.answer: $|\mathbf{v}|=5$, so the unit vector is $\left\langle\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle$. Scaling to length $10$: $10\left\langle\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle=\langle6,8\rangle$.

questions.q: Determine whether $\mathbf{u}=\langle2,-3,1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,2,4\rangle$ are orthogonal.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=2(1)+(-3)(2)+1(4)=2-6+4=0$. Since the dot product is $0$, they are orthogonal.

questions.q: For $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,-1,2\rangle$, find $|\mathbf{u}|$ and the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$.
questions.answer: $|\mathbf{u}|=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt{6}$. $\hat{\mathbf{u}}=\left\langle\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\right\rangle$.

questions.q: Find a value of $k$ so that $\mathbf{u}=\langle k,3\rangle$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{v}=\langle4,-2\rangle$.
questions.answer: Need $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$: $4k-6=0 \Rightarrow k=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

sections.heading: The triangle inequality and vector geometry

questions.q: State the Triangle Inequality for vectors.
questions.answer: For all vectors $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$: $|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}|+|\mathbf{v}|$.

questions.q: Verify the Triangle Inequality for $\mathbf{u}=\langle3,0\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle0,4\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\langle3,4\rangle$, so $|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|=5$. $|\mathbf{u}|+|\mathbf{v}|=3+4=7$. Since $5\leq7$, the inequality holds.

questions.q: The projection of $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$ is $\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}=\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\mathbf{v}$. Find $\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}$ for $\mathbf{u}=\langle3,4\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,0\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=3$, $|\mathbf{v}|^2=1$. $\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}=\dfrac{3}{1}\langle1,0\rangle=\langle3,0\rangle$.

questions.q: Find $\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}$ for $\mathbf{u}=\langle4,3\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,1\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=7$, $|\mathbf{v}|^2=2$. $\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}=\dfrac{7}{2}\langle1,1\rangle=\left\langle\dfrac{7}{2},\dfrac{7}{2}\right\rangle$.

questions.q: Write $\mathbf{w}=\langle7,4\rangle$ as a linear combination $a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}$ of $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle0,1\rangle$.
questions.answer: Since $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$ are the standard basis vectors, $\mathbf{w}=7\mathbf{u}+4\mathbf{v}$.

questions.q: Write $\mathbf{w}=\langle5,1\rangle$ as a linear combination $a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}$ of $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,-1\rangle$.
questions.answer: Need $a+b=5$ and $a-b=1$. Adding: $2a=6 \Rightarrow a=3$; then $b=2$. So $\mathbf{w}=3\mathbf{u}+2\mathbf{v}$.

questions.q: Explain briefly why every vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle1,-1\rangle$ (i.e., why they span $\mathbb{R}^2$).
questions.answer: $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are not parallel (neither is a scalar multiple of the other), so they point in two genuinely different directions in the plane. Two non-parallel vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ always span the whole plane, since any target vector's components along each direction can always be solved for (as in the two questions above, the resulting $2\times2$ system always has a unique solution).

questions.q: Is $\mathbf{w}=\langle3,6\rangle$ in the span of $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,2\rangle$ alone? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Yes: $\mathbf{w}=3\mathbf{u}$, since $3\langle1,2\rangle=\langle3,6\rangle$. A single nonzero vector's span is the entire line through the origin in its direction, and $\mathbf{w}$ lies on that line.

questions.q: Explain why $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,2\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle2,4\rangle$ do NOT span all of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{v}=2\mathbf{u}$, so $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are parallel — every linear combination $a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}=(a+2b)\mathbf{u}$ is just a scalar multiple of $\mathbf{u}$, so their span is only the line through the origin in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$, not the whole plane.

questions.q: Determine whether $\mathbf{w}=\langle1,1,1\rangle$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,0,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{v}=\langle0,1,0\rangle$.
questions.answer: No. Any combination $a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}=\langle a,b,0\rangle$ always has a $0$ in the third coordinate, but $\mathbf{w}$ has a $1$ there — so $\mathbf{w}$ is not in the span of $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$.

questions.q: Write $\mathbf{w}=\langle4,-1,7\rangle$ as a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,0,0\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle0,1,0\rangle$, and $\mathbf{z}=\langle0,0,1\rangle$, and explain why this is always possible for ANY vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
questions.answer: $\mathbf{w}=4\mathbf{u}-1\mathbf{v}+7\mathbf{z}$. This is always possible for any vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ because $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}$ are the standard basis vectors: every vector's own coordinates ARE exactly its coefficients in this combination, so $\{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}\}$ spans all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ by definition.

questions.q: How many vectors, at minimum, are needed to span $\mathbb{R}^n$? Justify briefly.
questions.answer: At least $n$ vectors are needed. Fewer than $n$ vectors can span at most a subspace of dimension less than $n$ (a proper subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$), so they cannot reach every vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$; the standard basis shows $n$ vectors suffice.

questions.q: Determine whether $\mathbf{u}=\langle1,2,-1\rangle$, $\mathbf{v}=\langle2,1,1\rangle$, and $\mathbf{w}=\langle3,3,0\rangle$ span $\mathbb{R}^3$, given that $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$.
questions.answer: No. Since $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$, $\mathbf{w}$ contributes no new direction beyond $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ — every linear combination $a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}+c\mathbf{w}=a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}+c(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=(a+c)\mathbf{u}+(b+c)\mathbf{v}$ is really just a combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ alone. Two vectors can span at most a 2-dimensional subspace (a plane through the origin) of $\mathbb{R}^3$, not the full three-dimensional space.

questions.q: Give an example of three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that DO span $\mathbb{R}^3$, and briefly justify why they work.
questions.answer: The standard basis $\mathbf{e}_1=\langle1,0,0\rangle$, $\mathbf{e}_2=\langle0,1,0\rangle$, $\mathbf{e}_3=\langle0,0,1\rangle$ works: any vector $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ equals $a\mathbf{e}_1+b\mathbf{e}_2+c\mathbf{e}_3$ directly, so every vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is reachable.

questions.q: Summarize in one sentence the difference between a set of vectors being linearly independent and a set of vectors spanning a space.
questions.answer: Spanning is about reaching every vector in the space (enough vectors, covering all directions); linear independence is about having no redundant vectors (none is a combination of the others) — a basis needs both properties at once.
